title: Slide 1 · Statistical Learning, Estimation, and Generalization
question: Recall the two rules. A predicts 10 × hours + 5 × sets + 25. B predicts 10 × hours + 6 × sets + 22. Why can Ava’s score alone never choose between them?
answer: On Ava, A gives 20 + 15 + 25 = 60 and B gives 20 + 18 + 22 = 60. Both make zero error. At one hour and one set they give 40 and 38. A score observed there could distinguish them. We also need to know how common inputs like that are.

title: Slide 2 · Whose next score will we predict?
question: If the intended population changes to all students taking a different exam, can we still treat the four rows as its full population?
answer: No. The four records describe the invented exam. A new exam could change both which students appear and how scores relate to preparation.

title: Slide 3 · Two rules can agree on Ava
question: If the training sample contains only Ava, can squared error choose between these rules?
answer: Both predictions equal 60. Each has zero training error. A preference between them would have to come from another observation or an assumption about the pattern.

title: Slide 4 · Turn individual misses into a sample average
question: The sample contains scores 56 and 66. What is the empirical squared risk of predicting 60 for both?
answer: The errors are 4 and −6. Average the squares to obtain (16 + 36)/2 = 26 squared points.

title: Slide 5 · Calculate the risk for the whole toy population
question: Keep the four scores fixed but make Ava the only case that ever occurs. What is each rule’s expected risk?
answer: The population now puts probability 1 on Ava and 0 elsewhere. Both rules predict Ava exactly, so both expected risks are zero.

title: Slide 6 · Why estimates vary between samples
question: If we always sample only the two students with the largest hours, what estimate do we get for the constant rule?
answer: Their losses are 0 and 36, so the estimate is 18. Repeating the same selection gives 18 again, even though the equally weighted population risk is 38.

title: Slide 7 · Separate choosing a rule from checking it
question: What goes wrong if you repeatedly choose a different rule after viewing the same test scores?
answer: The test results influence the rule. That set now helps select the model and can give an optimistic final estimate. An independent final evaluation needs fresh cases.

title: Slide 8 · Spot information that arrives too late
question: You want to predict a new student’s performance, but that student’s duplicate record appears in training. How would you split the data?
answer: Keep rows for the same student together and split by student. This makes the test student genuinely new. If the goal also involves future exams, preserve the timing when you choose the split.

title: Slide 9 · Turn Stage I into a learning procedure
question: What do hours contribute to the fitted constant prediction?
answer: Nothing. A class containing only constants treats all students alike. A line with a learned slope can use differences in hours.

title: Slide 11 · From this module to the next
question: A constant score ignores hours. What two quantities would let a straight line adapt to how hours and scores vary together?
answer: An intercept gives the prediction at zero hours. A slope gives the change in the predicted score for one more hour. Module 05 estimates both from training pairs.

title: Office hours · What does generalization mean for Ava’s example?
question: What does generalization mean for Ava’s example?
answer: A prediction rule generalizes well when it has low loss on the future records we care about. Lowering Ava’s loss proves that her prediction improved. Predicting for new students also requires evidence about those students, the time of prediction and which examples were excluded from fitting.

title: Office hours · Why learn from a sample if it can give the wrong answer?
question: Why learn from a sample if it can give the wrong answer?
answer: Measuring everyone is often impossible. A sample drawn to represent the target population can estimate average loss and help select a rule. Examining how much the estimate changes across samples tells us about its precision. Selective sampling can still distort it.

title: Office hours · Is the smallest training error always the best choice?
question: Is the smallest training error always the best choice?
answer: It identifies the best fit to those measurements under the chosen loss. A flexible rule can memorize observed values yet predict poorly elsewhere. Validation compares choices on fresh cases, and a separate test estimates the chosen procedure’s performance.

title: Exercise 1
question: A constant prediction of 12 meets observations 10, 11, 15. Write and compute its empirical squared risk.
answer: R̂(c) = [(c−10)²+(c−11)²+(c−15)²]/3. At c=12 the value is (4+1+9)/3 = 14/3 squared units.

title: Exercise 2
question: A rule loses 1 on ordinary cases and 9 on unusual cases. Future cases are 75% ordinary. Find expected loss and compare with a sample containing one of each.
answer: Population risk is 0.75×1+0.25×9=3. The balanced sample gives (1+9)/2=5 because unusual cases have a larger share in that sample.

title: Exercise 3
question: Two candidate rules predict 70 on every training record. At a new input they predict 65 and 85. What evidence would discriminate between them?
answer: A labeled case on which they differ lets us compare losses. More such independently sampled cases better represent which inputs matter. Agreement on training records alone cannot break the tie.

title: Exercise 4
question: You fit twenty models and report the smallest of twenty test errors on the same students. Redesign the evaluation.
answer: The so-called test set selected the winner. Fit on training data, choose among twenty using validation data, then evaluate that single choice on untouched students sampled for the prediction goal.

title: Exercise 5
question: A score predictor uses a retake invitation sent after grading. Its held-out error is tiny. What is the first check?
answer: If the goal is a prediction before the exam, the invitation arrives too late. Remove it, rebuild training features as of prediction time, and rerun the evaluation.

title: Exercise 6
question: Two independent small samples give estimates 12 and 18. Does the difference alone show that one estimate was computed incorrectly?
answer: No. Different sampled cases may contribute different individual losses. Check the arithmetic, sample selection and variation before attributing the difference to a mistake.
